questions.passage:
How much should we care about people who are not yet born? The question sounds philosophical, but economists answer it every time they evaluate a policy whose costs fall now and whose benefits arrive decades hence, and the answer is encoded in a single number, the discount rate. Discounting converts future sums into present equivalents: at a rate of 5 per cent a year, a benefit of a hundred rupees in thirty years is worth about twenty-three rupees today, and at 1 per cent it is worth about seventy-four. For a project whose payoffs last for centuries, as with measures against climate change, the choice of rate can make the difference between a policy that looks wildly profitable and one that looks absurdly expensive.

The dispute became public with the Stern Review of 2006, which argued for urgent and costly action on emissions and used a very low discount rate, about 1.4 per cent a year. William Nordhaus, a leading climate economist whose own integrated model had recommended a gradual tightening of controls, replied that Stern’s conclusions were driven almost entirely by this assumption: with a rate closer to those observed in financial markets, the same damages would justify far more modest action. Neither side disputed the climate science. They disagreed about what the rate should represent.

The standard formula, associated with Frank Ramsey, breaks the rate into two parts. The first is pure time preference, the degree to which we value a given benefit less simply because it comes later. The second reflects the fact that if the economy keeps growing, future people will be richer than we are, so that an extra rupee matters less to them than it does to us; this part depends on the expected growth rate and on how fast the value of an extra unit of consumption falls as people get richer. Stern set pure time preference close to zero on the ground that it is ethically indefensible to count the welfare of a person for less merely because of when she is born. Nordhaus argued that a rate in line with observed market returns reveals how people actually trade off the present against the future, and that policy should respect those preferences.

Each position has a weakness. The market-rate view treats observed interest rates as a window into society’s ethical judgement about future generations, but market rates reflect the preferences of the people who are alive and who choose between their own consumption now and later, not the interests of those who cannot take part in the market. Moreover, the market contains many rates, from those on safe government bonds to those on risky equities, and which one is relevant depends on the risk of the project, itself a contested matter. The ethical view, on the other hand, runs into the problem that a very low discount rate can demand enormous sacrifices by the present generation on behalf of the future: if the rate is nearly zero, almost any investment with a positive return over a long horizon is justified, and the poor of today, who are poorer than the future rich, are asked to sacrifice for those who will be much better off.

The growth assumption in the second part of the formula carries its own difficulty. If climate damage is severe enough to reduce growth, then future people will not be richer, and the premise that justifies a positive discount rate weakens in precisely the scenarios that policy is meant to avoid. This has led economists to argue that the discount rate itself should be uncertain and should decline over long horizons: if we do not know how fast the economy will grow, the possibility of low growth, which makes future benefits more valuable, should receive weight, and the weighted average rate falls as the horizon lengthens. Several governments, including the United Kingdom and France, have adopted schedules with declining rates for long-lived projects. The effect is considerable: a benefit two centuries away is discounted far less than under a constant rate.

A deeper objection is that discounting is the wrong tool for some damages. Money can be traded across time, but not all losses are fungible with it. The extinction of a species, the loss of a coral reef or the collapse of an ice sheet may be irreversible, and if future people value these things in ways that cannot be compensated by greater income, then treating the damage as a sum to be discounted misdescribes it. Defenders of discounting reply that refusing to discount at all merely hides the trade-offs: resources spent on avoiding one remote catastrophe are unavailable for others, including present poverty, health and education, and a policy of infinite concern for the future is a policy of paralysis in the present.

Some philosophers go further and deny that the framework of weighing costs against benefits is appropriate at all. On a rights-based view, the present generation has a duty not to impose serious harm on the future, whatever the price of avoiding it, just as one may not poison a neighbour’s well because the saving is large. Such a view avoids the problem of the discount rate by refusing to trade, but it has its own difficulty of saying where the duty ends: almost every activity imposes some risk on future people, and a duty without limit cannot guide action.

The upshot is that the discount rate is not a scientific parameter waiting to be measured but a place where ethical judgement and empirical forecast meet. The empirical part concerns growth, risk and the substitutability of environmental goods; the ethical part concerns whether time itself should matter. Making the choice transparent, and reporting results under a range of rates, is more honest than hiding it inside a single number presented as a fact. Whatever rate is chosen, it will encode an answer to the question with which this essay began, and a society that does not know what answer it has given has not avoided the question.
questions.question: The author’s statement that Stern and Nordhaus did not dispute the climate science implies that:
options: A) Stern and Nordhaus agreed on the policy that should be adopted, and disagreed only about the language in which to describe it to the public
B) the discount rate is a scientific quantity that Stern had measured incorrectly and that Nordhaus corrected using data from financial markets
C) the climate damages estimated by the two economists were identical, so that the choice of rate could not have affected their results at all
D) their differing conclusions flowed chiefly from differing assumptions about how future benefits should be valued
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 2: both accepted the science; they disagreed about what the rate should represent, and Nordhaus said Stern’s conclusions were driven almost entirely by his low rate. The other options claim policy agreement, a measurable ‘correct’ rate, or identical damages, none of which the passage says.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken Nordhaus’s argument that observed market rates should guide the choice of discount rate?
options: A) Most people, when asked about the welfare of future generations, give weights far higher than those implied by market interest rates.
B) Market interest rates have been stable over the past century and have varied little between countries with different levels of income.
C) Stern’s review rested on estimates of climate damage that were later revised downward by many of the leading climate scientists.
D) Economic growth over the next century is likely to be faster than in the past, which would make future generations richer than we are.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Nordhaus holds that market rates reveal how people trade off present and future. If people’s stated valuation of future generations differs sharply from market rates, the rates are a poor guide to that valuation. The other options concern stability, Stern’s estimates, or growth (which, if anything, supports a positive rate).

questions.question: The author’s remark that a near-zero discount rate can ask “the poor of today” to sacrifice implies that:
options: A) the poor of today will be richer than future generations and so ought to bear the costs of protecting the climate for those who follow
B) a low discount rate is justified only if the present generation is wealthier than all of the generations that will follow it in time
C) an ethical argument for treating all generations equally can conflict with concern for the present poor
D) the discount rate should be set at the level that makes present sacrifices exactly equal to future benefits in every case that arises
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 4: with a near-zero rate almost any long-horizon investment is justified, so the present poor, who are poorer than the future rich, are asked to sacrifice for them. This is a conflict between equal concern for all generations and concern for the present poor. The other options reverse or invent claims.

Under such incentives, even honest researchers will produce unreliable results in the aggregate, as practices that improve the chances of publication spread through a field without anyone intending them to. Reform therefore requires changing what is rewarded: valuing methodological rigour, publishing null results, and treating replication as a contribution rather than an affront. A technical fix without a change of incentives will tend to be absorbed, as other measures have been, by a system adapting to preserve what it rewards.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author’s overall position?
options: A) Science is fundamentally broken, and published findings should be disregarded until the whole system of research is rebuilt from scratch
B) The replication crisis is a result of fraud, and would end if researchers who cheat were identified and expelled from science entirely
C) Statistical significance is a meaningless concept, and should be abandoned in favour of the judgement of expert reviewers alone
D) Single studies are weak evidence, so confidence should rest on patterns confirmed across independent studies and on better incentives
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraphs 6 and 7: the crisis shows that single studies are weak evidence, confidence should attach to patterns across independent studies, and reform needs a change of incentives. The author rejects the claims that science is broken or that fraud is the cause.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. When the water becomes too warm, the corals expel the algae and turn white, an event known as bleaching.
2. Coral reefs cover a tiny fraction of the ocean floor but support a large share of marine species.
3. Prolonged bleaching can kill the coral, and with it the habitat on which the reef’s other species depend.
4. Their richness depends on a partnership between coral animals and microscopic algae that live inside them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 introduces reefs, 4 (‘their richness’) explains the partnership behind it, 1 describes what happens when the partnership breaks, and 3 gives the consequence of prolonged bleaching.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Not every promise qualifies, however, since courts require that each party give something of value in return.
2. A promise to give a gift, however sincere, is therefore generally not enforceable in a court of law.
3. A contract is a promise that the law will enforce.
4. This requirement, known as consideration, separates binding bargains from mere gifts.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 defines a contract, 1 (‘however’) limits which promises count, 4 (‘this requirement’) names it, and 2 (‘therefore’) applies it to gifts.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Hayek argued that this dispersed, self-adjusting knowledge is what planned economies cannot replicate.
2. No central planner needs to know why the crop failed for this adjustment to occur.
3. When a crop fails, its price rises, signalling consumers to economise and producers to supply more.
4. Prices in a market economy convey information about scarcity.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 states the general claim, 3 gives the example, 2 (‘this adjustment’) draws out the point about planners, and 1 (‘this dispersed… knowledge’) attributes the conclusion to Hayek.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Sleep is not a passive state in which the brain simply switches off.
2. During deep sleep the brain consolidates memories, transferring recent experiences into longer-term storage.
3. Students who sacrifice sleep to revise may thus defeat the purpose of their effort.
4. Chronic sleep deprivation therefore impairs learning, even when the hours of study are unchanged.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 1 states the claim, 2 gives the mechanism, 4 (‘therefore’) draws the first consequence, and 3 (‘thus’) applies it to students.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Literacy, which had been confined largely to clergy and administrators, began to spread among merchants and craftsmen.
2. The printing press made books cheaper and more widely available in the fifteenth century.
3. A reading public of this kind created a demand for works in vernacular languages rather than in Latin.
4. In time, the standardisation of printed vernaculars helped to shape national identities.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states the technological change, 1 describes the spread of literacy, 3 (‘a reading public of this kind’) the demand for vernacular books, and 4 (‘in time’) the long-term outcome.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Kahneman and Tversky found that people systematically underestimate the time, cost and risk of future projects, even when they know that similar past projects overran. The “inside view” focuses on the specifics of the plan at hand; the “outside view” consults the record of comparable projects. Organisations that adopt reference class forecasting reduce overruns, but political incentives to promote projects often reward optimism.'
options: A) Planning is futile because projects always overrun, and organisations should therefore stop forecasting costs and durations altogether in practice.
B) People underestimate project costs only when they lack experience, and reference class forecasting has been shown to eliminate overruns completely.
C) People underestimate cost and time through an inside view; the record of comparable projects helps, though incentives favour optimism.
D) The outside view relies on the details of a plan, whereas the inside view uses the record of similar projects completed by other organisations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph describes the planning fallacy, the remedy of the outside view, and the incentive problem. The distractors say planning is futile, claim the remedy eliminates overruns, or swap the two views.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Rawls asked what principles of justice people would choose if they did not know their own position in society, whether rich or poor, talented or not. Behind such a “veil of ignorance”, he argued, rational people would choose principles that protect the worst-off, since they might be among them. Critics reply that the thought experiment smuggles in risk-aversion: people more willing to gamble might choose differently, so the conclusion may depend on psychological assumptions rather than pure reason.'
options: A) Behind a veil of ignorance people might protect the worst-off, though critics say this rests on risk-aversion.
B) Rawls proved that rational people would always choose equal distribution of income, whatever their attitude to taking risks in life.
C) The veil of ignorance shows that justice is purely a matter of psychology, so that no argument about it can be rational at all.
D) Critics have shown that people behind the veil would choose to favour the rich, since they might be among the wealthy members of society.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph reports Rawls’s argument and the critics’ objection about risk-aversion. The other options overstate it (‘proved’, ‘always’), say justice is merely psychology, or reverse the critics’ point.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Studies show that the first number mentioned in a negotiation pulls the final settlement towards it, even when the number is arbitrary. Experts are not immune: estate agents’ valuations of a house were swayed by the listed price. Negotiators therefore often try to make the first offer, though doing so can reveal information, and the benefit depends on the offer being credible rather than absurd.'
options: A) Anchoring affects only novices, because experts such as estate agents are immune to arbitrary numbers in their valuations of property.
B) The first number in a negotiation tends to anchor the outcome, so opening offers matter if they remain credible.
C) Making the first offer is always the best strategy, since it never reveals any information to the other party in a bargaining.
D) Negotiated outcomes are determined entirely by the arbitrary numbers mentioned at the start, whatever the offers that follow them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph describes anchoring, the susceptibility of experts, and the caveats about information and credibility. The distractors say experts are immune, that first offers are always best, or that anchors determine outcomes entirely.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A vaccine that prevents severe disease but not infection still reduces hospital admissions. It would, however, be a poor basis for a strategy of herd immunity, because ________.'
options: A) it prevents hospital admissions, which are irrelevant to the spread of the virus through the community as a whole and its effects
B) herd immunity is achieved only when everyone is infected, whether or not they have been vaccinated against the disease concerned
C) severe disease occurs only in the elderly, so that vaccinating the young would have no effect on the population at large
D) vaccinated people can still transmit the virus, so its spread through the population is not stopped
questions.explanation: Explanation: Herd immunity depends on stopping transmission; a vaccine that prevents severe disease but not infection leaves transmission largely unchecked. The other options misstate the relevance of admissions, the definition of herd immunity, or the distribution of disease.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Economists describe goods that are neither excludable nor rivalrous as public goods. Because nobody can be stopped from enjoying them, private firms have little incentive to supply them, and so ________.'
options: A) they are always supplied in excess, since firms compete to provide them to as many consumers as possible in the market
B) consumers value them less than private goods, which is why governments rarely devote resources to providing them to citizens
C) they are usually funded collectively, through taxation or public provision
D) firms provide them at very high prices, since consumers have no alternative source from which to obtain them at all
questions.explanation: Explanation: Free-riding discourages private supply, so public goods are typically provided through collective funding. The other options contradict the premise (excess supply, high private prices) or invent a claim about consumer valuation.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'VERACITY':
options: A) Honesty
B) Duplicity
C) Frivolity
D) Brevity
questions.explanation: Explanation: Veracity means truthfulness; 'honesty' is closest. 'Duplicity' is its opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'INSIPID':
options: A) Bland
B) Piquant
C) Dull
D) Tasteless
questions.explanation: Explanation: Insipid means lacking flavour or interest; 'piquant' (pleasantly sharp, stimulating) is the antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'SANCTIMONIOUS':
options: A) Humble
B) Candid
C) Priggish
D) Genial
questions.explanation: Explanation: Sanctimonious means making a show of moral superiority; 'priggish' (self-righteously moralistic) is closest. 'Humble' is the opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'TRUNCATE':
options: A) Curtail
B) Shorten
C) Abridge
D) Extend
questions.explanation: Explanation: Truncate means to shorten by cutting off; 'extend' is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'CACOPHONY':
options: A) Din
B) Harmony
C) Silence
D) Melody
questions.explanation: Explanation: Cacophony means a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds; 'din' is closest. The others are opposites.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The senator’s ________ speech, full of high-minded phrases and empty of proposals, impressed no one.'
options: A) understated
B) bombastic
C) unpretentious
D) succinct
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Bombastic' means high-sounding but with little meaning. The others describe plain or brief speech.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'The new law was widely ________ as a step forward, though its critics found it ________ in its details.'
options: A) condemned; severe
B) ignored; popular
C) hailed; vague
D) welcomed; praised
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Hailed as a step forward... though critics found it vague' gives a coherent contrast. The other pairs fail the contrast or are illogical with 'though'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct idiom meaning:
'To throw caution to the wind' means to:
options: A) distribute resources among those who need them
B) proceed slowly in order to avoid any mistakes
C) leave a difficult decision to somebody else
D) act recklessly, ignoring the risks
questions.explanation: Explanation: The image is of discarding care; the idiom means acting without regard to danger.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which the word 'COMPLEMENT' is used correctly:
options: A) The wine was a perfect complement to the meal.
B) She received a complement on her speech from the director.
C) He paid her a generous complement on her excellent performance.
D) The teacher’s complement made the whole class happy.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Complement' means something that completes or goes well with another; praise is a 'compliment'. Only the wine sentence is correct.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'Ten kilometres ________ a long distance to walk.'
options: A) are
B) is
C) were
D) have been
questions.explanation: Explanation: A distance treated as a single unit takes a singular verb: 'is'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'The boy (A) / whom I thought (B) / was honest (C) / has deceived me (D).'
options: A) The boy
B) whom I thought
C) was honest
D) has deceived me
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Who' is the subject of 'was honest'; 'I thought' is parenthetical. So the correct form is 'who I thought was honest'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) I look forward to meet you soon.
B) I look forward to have met you.
C) I look forward to meeting you.
D) I look forward to be meeting you.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition and is followed by a gerund: 'meeting'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'He ________ the guitar for five years before he joined the band.'
options: A) had been playing
B) was playing
C) would have been playing
D) has played
questions.explanation: Explanation: A continuous action that continued up to an earlier past point takes the past perfect continuous: 'had been playing'.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) The prize was divided between the three finalists.
B) The prize was divided in between all three finalists.
C) The prize was divided among the three finalists.
D) The prize was divided amongst between the three finalists.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Among' is used for more than two; 'between' is used for two. The other options are incorrect or redundant.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'Not only (A) / the students but also (B) / the teacher (C) / were present (D).'
options: A) Not only
B) the students but also
C) the teacher
D) were present
questions.explanation: Explanation: With 'not only... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the teacher' (singular): 'was present'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'She was accused ________ stealing the necklace.'
options: A) for
B) of
C) with
D) on
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Accuse' takes 'of': 'accused of stealing'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) I have known him since childhood and he has not changed.
B) She has been working here since last year without a break.
C) They have lived in this city for more than twenty years now.
D) I am knowing him since childhood.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Stative verbs like 'know' are not used in continuous tenses, and 'since' with a period requires the present perfect: 'I have known him since childhood'.
